I've been using various versions of Windows since I was a child, mostly 98, 2000, XP and 8. We've all heard the common belief that Windows ME and Vista were the worst ones ever, and that XP and 7 were the best ones Microsoft put out.

When I finally got my own laptop, it was in mid 2013, after pretty much every manufacturer stopped pairing Windows 7 with their products in favor of Win8. I had used Windows 7 quite a bit in school, and aside from the absence of a Start menu I felt like Windows 8 was just the Windows 7 platform with a new skin over it (similar to the progression from Win2k to XP). However I soon learned how Microsoft was vigilantly trying to bring Windows far away from its predecessors (removing code that had existed since Win95, etc...)

I have never in my life had so many problems with a computer than with Windows 8, and possibly even more with 8.1. For the first few months everything worked pretty well, but when I updated to 8.1 my audio driver started sounding distorted. Then came the corrupted files that mysteriously disappear yet still take up space on my SSD. I formatted and reinstalled 8 and within a month, like clockwork, those exact same problems came back. Then I tried my 'free' copy of Windows 10, which unactivates itself half of the time, leaving me unable to change my wallpaper, themes, etc... Programs freeze and I cannot end their processes because "access is denied" with no explanation.

I know there is nothing wrong with my computer because I have used multiple Linux distro's on it over the course of owning it, with no problems with my audio, SSD, processor, or anything else. Not a single one. Ever.

What I want to know is if anyone else feels that the quality of Windows Operating Systems has fallen in the past ~7 years, because I can't help but feel that is the case. Windows XP still runs flawless to this day, even with its inherent security concerns. Every single Windows 7 machine I've used has not had a single problem. Am I just having really, really bad luck with Windows 8/8.1 & 10? I literally back up my data every other day for fear of losing everything once again.
Was Win7 the peak of Windows' reliability?

Win 7 was everything Vista should have been. Vista was a bloated POS. 7 took Vista's strengths and took away it's weaknesses. 7 would have been the next XP (well, it really is in fact). I jumped straight from XP to 7 and loved it. My current machine came with 8.1 and so far, I haven't had any real troubles with it. It sometimes feels like it takes things a bit longer to launch than I think they should (and I've got 8GB of RAM) but I hated having to work on 8. 8.1 seems to be better. At least my machine came from the factory defaulting to the normal desktop mode. I never even look at the 'Metro' screens unless some default Metro app launches itself. 10 has just been god awful, even with machines that came with it pre-installed. I fought for hours to get my daughter's 10 laptop up and running to where her Onedrive files would start syncing down to the machine.

I have a theory that when MS said 10 was going to be the last version of Windows, maybe they really meant it and will eventually move on to a completely new system like Apple did back in 2000 or so. MS has no hope at this point of having and maintaining this 'convergence' mode that they're going for. PC gamers won't want to purchase a game from the MS store as it will be hobbled by having to also conform to the Xbox One version, people who have an Xbox probably have no desire to have integration with their PC, and the Windows Phone market continues to shrink. MS needs to bite the bullet, pick a Linux or BSD distro, tack on some backwards compatibility for a few years (hell, most of the work has been done for them already), and leave all this legacy crap behind. 10 is more than likely less secure than every version of Windows that came before it in that it's only a matter of time before someone comes up with some script or virus that hijacks all the Telemetry and personal info that goes along with it. 7 was/is the last, most perfected version of Windows ever produced. But it's time to move on. It kills me to think that at one point, MS had a version of Unix they were selling called Xenix, but they decided to go with their own in house NT system. Had they learned from the Unix culture some proper security measures, we wouldn't have half the problems we do today. No system is perfect, every lock can be picked, but when your idea of security is akin to a screen door on a submarine, well, you're fucked.
